extracted.intended_audience: editors, publishers, researchers, and scholarly-publishing professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and reason about system-level and actor-level ethical issues in scholarly publishing. The piece highlights dimensions beyond individual checklists—culture, transparency, legal accountability, dynamics of standards, and ecosystem incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diverse factors shape ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethical standards could be as diverse as the publishing ecosystem itself — guided and determined by norms, cultures, beliefs, logic/cognitive thinking, values, legacies, and resistance to change of a discipline, community, society, country, or region.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating ethics, consider local and disciplinary norms and historical practices rather than assuming a single universal standard. Examples: some may not regard accessing pirated articles as unethical; asking for a PDF via social media may be seen as equivalent to an earlier-era reprint request; paying peer reviewers is viewed as a conflict of interest in many Global North journals but is routine in parts of the Global South. Watch for localized practices such as gift authorship, groups rotating authorship to boost counts, or illicit markets selling authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical standards are dynamic
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards change over time (e.g., submission of unpublished manuscripts vs. preprints; confidentiality of reviewers’ comments vs. open review; evolving policies on allowable AI use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess policies and practices for responsiveness to change and take into account that what was unacceptable previously may now be accepted (and vice versa). Evaluate whether journals, publishers, and institutions update policies transparently and consistently—examples include acceptance of preprints, praising public disclosure of reviewer identities/comments, and ongoing debates about AI use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not being transparent isn’t considered unethical
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of transparency (for example, publishers remaining secretive about APC calculations) is often tolerated; stakeholders frequently trust publishers’ opaque claims and pay high fees without comparative procurement-like scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include transparency of costs, decision-making, and editorial/production processes as a core ethical criterion. Look for explicit APC breakdowns, justification of pricing relative to journal metrics, and institutional practices for vetting and comparing publication venues. Absence of transparency can hide value capture by journals and publishers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal offenses hide behind ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Some unethical publishing practices may mask or overlap with criminal behavior — e.g., journals that built brands to attract APCs but were delisted for failing production/editorial standards; fake/hijacked journals, papermills, and managers selling authorship may amount to criminal activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing misconduct, consider whether harms could be actionable (violation of trust, fraud) and which legal or regulatory remedies exist. Use indicators such as delisting from indexes (Clarivate/Scopus) as signals of serious failure, and question who bears financial and reputational costs and what recourse authors and institutions might have.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly ecosystem nurtures unethical practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Structural incentives of the academic system (e.g., publish-or-perish, emphasis on quantity over quality, commodification of research communication) create conditions that enable and sustain unethical practices across publishers, institutions, and researchers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate ethics not only at the individual or journal level but across the system: assess incentive structures, volume-driven metrics, indexing practices, and weak remediation (e.g., lower ranking or temporary delisting as the main sanction). Consider measures that address systemic drivers—research culture change, governance, accountability, and reforms to reward quality and integrity rather than sheer output.
